title: What Is BAC? Blood Alcohol Content Levels and What Each Feels Like
excerpt: What blood alcohol content (BAC) means, what each level from 0.02% to 0.40% feels like, legal limits, how to estimate yours, how long it takes to go down, and when BAC becomes an emergency.
metaDescription: What is BAC? Blood alcohol content explained: how each level feels, legal limits, how to estimate it, how fast it drops, and when it's an emergency.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The short answer:** BAC, or blood alcohol content (also called blood alcohol concentration), is the share of your blood that is alcohol. A BAC of 0.08% means there are 0.08 grams of alcohol in every 100 milliliters of blood, or roughly one part alcohol per 1,250 parts blood. That sounds tiny, but it's enough to slow your reactions, blur your judgment, and make it illegal to drive in every US state. Your BAC climbs as you drink faster than your liver can keep up, peaks somewhere between 30 and 90 minutes after your last drink, and then falls at a fairly steady rate of about 0.015% per hour. Nothing you can buy or do speeds that fall up in a meaningful way.

This guide explains what the numbers mean, what each level actually feels like, why two people drinking the same thing can end up with very different readings, how to estimate your own BAC, and the signs that someone's BAC has climbed into dangerous territory.

> **When to get help right away.** Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone who has been drinking is confused or can't be woken, is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, has slow or irregular breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute, or gaps of 10 seconds or more), has a seizure, or has pale, bluish, or cold, clammy skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, which means BAC is high enough to shut down basic functions like breathing and the gag reflex. Don't leave them to "sleep it off." Keep them on their side, stay with them, and get help. BAC can keep rising after someone passes out, because alcohol already in the stomach is still being absorbed.

## What Is BAC? Blood Alcohol Content Explained

When you drink, alcohol (ethanol) passes from your stomach and small intestine straight into your bloodstream. It isn't digested first the way food is. Once it's in your blood, it spreads into almost all the water in your body, including your brain, which is where the effects you feel come from.

Blood alcohol content is simply a measure of how concentrated that alcohol is in your blood at a given moment. It's the number police, doctors, and researchers use because it tracks closely with how impaired someone is. Two drinks mean very different things for a 120-pound person and a 220-pound person, but a BAC of 0.08% means roughly the same level of impairment for both.

A few things are worth knowing about the number itself:

- **It's a snapshot.** Your BAC is always moving. It rises while alcohol is being absorbed and falls as your liver breaks it down. A reading only tells you where you are right now.
- **It lags behind your drinking.** The drink you just finished hasn't fully hit your blood yet. That lag is why people often feel fine, have "one more," and then feel much drunker 45 minutes later.
- **It doesn't measure tolerance.** Someone who drinks often may *feel* less drunk at 0.08%, but their reaction time and judgment are still impaired. Tolerance hides the feeling more than the impairment.

## Blood Alcohol Concentration vs. Blood Alcohol Content: Is There a Difference?

No. "Blood alcohol content" and "blood alcohol concentration" are two names for the same measurement, and both are shortened to BAC. "Concentration" is the more technically accurate term and is what you'll see in medical and government sources. "Content" is what most people type into Google. You'll also see "blood alcohol level," which means the same thing.

You may run into a few related terms:

- **BrAC (breath alcohol concentration).** What a breathalyzer measures. It's alcohol in your breath, which is then converted to an estimated BAC. More on how that works below.
- **Per mille (‰) or promille.** Many European countries express BAC as grams per liter of blood, or parts per thousand. A BAC of 0.05% is the same as 0.5‰. If a European friend says the driving limit is "point five," they mean 0.05%.
- **mg/dL or mg/100 mL.** Hospital blood tests often report alcohol in milligrams per deciliter. A result of 80 mg/dL equals a BAC of 0.08%.

## How BAC Is Measured: Blood Tests, Breathalyzers, and Estimates

### Blood tests

A blood draw is the most direct way to measure BAC. Hospitals use it when treating someone who may have alcohol poisoning, and police may use it after a crash or when a breath test isn't possible. Note that hospitals often test serum (the liquid part of blood) rather than whole blood, which reads somewhat higher, so a hospital number and a forensic number aren't always directly comparable.

### Breathalyzers

Breath testing works because some of the alcohol in your blood passes into the air in your lungs. In the US, breath devices are calibrated on the assumption that the alcohol in 2,100 milliliters of deep-lung air matches the alcohol in 1 milliliter of blood (the 2,100-to-1 ratio). The device measures your breath and converts it to an estimated BAC.

That conversion is a standard assumption, not a law of nature. The real ratio varies from person to person and moment to moment, which is one reason roadside readings can differ from a blood test taken a little later. Recent drinking, burping, or vomiting can also leave alcohol in the mouth that inflates a reading for a short time, which is why official tests include a waiting period before the breath sample.

Personal breathalyzers are widely sold. Better ones (usually fuel-cell types) can give a reasonable ballpark, while cheap ones can be far off. Treat any home reading as a rough guide, never as permission to drive.

### Estimates and calculators

Most online BAC calculators use a version of the **Widmark formula**, developed by Swedish scientist Erik Widmark in the early 20th century. It estimates BAC from how much alcohol you drank, your body weight, your sex, and how long you've been drinking. It's useful for understanding how the pieces fit together, but it can't account for food, health, medications, or how fast you drank. We'll walk through it in a later section.

## What Each BAC Level Feels Like

This is the question most people are really asking. The descriptions below draw on the effects listed by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and other public health sources. Everyone is a little different, and regular drinkers may feel less at a given level, but the impairment underneath is broadly similar.

| BAC | What it typically feels like | What's actually impaired |
|---|---|---|
| 0.02% | Relaxed, slightly warm, mood a bit lifted | Some loss of judgment; harder to do two things at once; visual tracking starts to slip |
| 0.05% | Loosened up, louder, more talkative, less inhibited | Lowered alertness, slower reactions, reduced coordination; harder to track moving objects |
| 0.08% | Noticeably buzzed or tipsy; "I'm fine" feels true but isn't | Poor muscle coordination, worse reasoning and memory, hard to judge speed and distance; legal limit for driving in the US |
| 0.10% | Clearly drunk; may slur, sway, or repeat yourself | Reaction time clearly worse; slowed thinking; poor control of a vehicle |
| 0.15% | Very drunk; trouble standing or walking straight; nausea likely | Major loss of balance and muscle control; vomiting possible |
| 0.20% | Confused, disoriented; may need help to stand | Memory blackouts become likely; risk of choking on vomit rises |
| 0.30% | Stupor; may drift in and out of consciousness | Danger zone: breathing and gag reflex can be suppressed |
| 0.40% and up | Unconscious or unresponsive | Life-threatening; coma and death are possible |

### 0.01% to 0.03%: The first drink

At this level most people feel a mild lift: a bit more relaxed, a little warmer, slightly more talkative. It's subtle enough that many people would say they feel nothing at all. But research on driving and divided attention finds that small declines start here, especially in tasks that require doing two things at once, like steering while scanning for hazards.

### 0.04% to 0.06%: The "social buzz"

This is where alcohol's disinhibiting effects show up. People get louder, laugh more easily, and feel more confident. It's the level many social drinkers aim for without realizing it. It's also where judgment starts to slip in ways you don't notice from the inside. Many countries, including much of Europe, Australia, and Utah in the US, set their driving limit at 0.05% because crash risk is already measurably higher here.

### 0.07% to 0.09%: The legal limit

At 0.08%, coordination, balance, reaction time, and the ability to judge speed and distance are all noticeably affected. Many people feel "a little drunk" but still capable. This is the trap: the part of your brain that would judge whether you're impaired is itself impaired. The US set 0.08% as the national driving standard, but it isn't the line where impairment begins. It's the line where the law draws it.

### 0.10% to 0.12%: Clearly drunk

Speech may be slurred, balance is shaky, and thinking is slower. Most people around you would describe you as drunk. Emotional swings are common, and decisions you'd normally reject (texting an ex, another round of shots, driving) seem reasonable.

### 0.13% to 0.20%: Sloppy and sick

Above about 0.13%, the pleasant effects mostly give way to unpleasant ones. Coordination is poor, nausea and vomiting become likely, and the room may start to spin when you lie down (here's [why you get the drunk spins and how to stop them](/never-hungover/drunk-spins)). Around 0.20% many people begin to have blackouts, meaning the brain stops forming new memories even though the person is still awake, walking, and talking.

### 0.25% to 0.30%: Danger zone

At this point alcohol is depressing the parts of the brain that control basic survival functions. A person may be stuporous, unable to stand, or drifting in and out of consciousness. The gag reflex can weaken, so vomiting while semi-conscious can lead to choking. This is alcohol poisoning territory, and it needs medical attention.

### 0.35% and higher: Life-threatening

At these levels, breathing can slow or stop, body temperature can drop, and the heart rhythm can be affected. Coma and death are real risks. People who drink heavily every day can sometimes be awake at levels that would knock out a social drinker, but that doesn't make the level safe for them either.

## Legal BAC Limits: Driving and Beyond

Legal limits vary by place and by who is driving. As of this writing:

- **United States:** 0.08% for drivers 21 and over in every state except Utah, which lowered its limit to 0.05% in 2018.
- **Commercial drivers (US):** 0.04% for people driving trucks, buses, and other commercial vehicles.
- **Drivers under 21 (US):** Every state has "zero tolerance" laws that set the limit at or near zero, typically 0.00% to 0.02%.
- **Many other countries:** 0.05% is common across much of Europe and in Australia. Some countries set lower limits, and a few set the limit at or near zero.
- **United Kingdom:** 0.08% in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland; 0.05% in Scotland.

Laws change, and penalties can apply below the limit if you're judged to be impaired, so check the current rules where you live and where you're traveling. Limits also often apply to boating, and many workplaces have their own rules.

The simplest rule is the one most safety groups give: if you've been drinking, don't drive. There's no BAC calculator accurate enough to tell you you're safe to get behind the wheel.

## Why the Same Drinks Give Different People Different BACs

Two people can drink exactly the same thing at the same pace and end up with very different BACs. The main reasons:

### Body size and body water

Alcohol spreads through the water in your body. A larger person has more water to dilute the same amount of alcohol, so their BAC rises less per drink. Muscle holds more water than fat, so a person with more muscle at the same weight will also tend to reach a lower BAC.

### Sex

On average, women reach a higher BAC than men from the same number of drinks, even at the same weight. Part of the reason is that women, on average, have a lower proportion of body water. Some research also suggests differences in how much alcohol is broken down in the stomach before it reaches the blood. Hormonal shifts across the menstrual cycle may play a smaller role. This is an average, not a rule about any one person.

### Food in your stomach

This is one of the biggest factors you control. Food, especially a full meal, slows the rate at which your stomach empties into your small intestine, which is where most alcohol is absorbed. That spreads absorption out and lowers the peak BAC. Drinking on an empty stomach does the opposite: alcohol rushes in and your BAC spikes higher and faster. We cover this in detail in our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach).

### How fast you drink

Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed rate. If you drink faster than that, alcohol stacks up in your blood. Four drinks over four hours and four drinks in one hour lead to very different peaks, even though the total is the same.

### What you're drinking

The strength of the drink matters more than the type. A "beer" can be a 4% light lager or a 10% imperial stout, and a mixed drink can easily hold two or three shots. Carbonation may speed absorption slightly in some people, which is one reason champagne and drinks mixed with soda can seem to "hit faster," though the effect varies.

### Medications and health

Some medications slow alcohol breakdown or add to its sedating effects, and liver disease can change how alcohol is processed. If you take regular medication, ask your pharmacist how it interacts with alcohol.

### Genetics

Variations in the enzymes that break down alcohol affect how people react to it. The best-known example is the ALDH2 variant common in people of East Asian descent, which causes facial flushing, a fast heartbeat, and nausea after drinking because a toxic by-product called acetaldehyde builds up. (Our [Asian flush guide](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) explains this in depth.) Genetics changes how alcohol feels and how harmful it is more than it changes the BAC reading itself.

## What Counts as a "Drink"? The Standard Drink

BAC estimates are built on the idea of a **standard drink**. In the US, the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) defines one standard drink as any drink containing about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's roughly:

- 12 ounces of regular beer at about 5% alcohol
- 5 ounces of wine at about 12% alcohol
- 1.5 ounces (one shot) of 80-proof spirits at about 40% alcohol

Real drinks often don't match. A pint of 7% IPA is closer to two standard drinks. A generous restaurant pour of wine can be 6 to 9 ounces. A margarita or Long Island iced tea can hold the equivalent of two to four standard drinks. If you're trying to estimate your BAC, count the alcohol, not the glasses.

Other countries define a standard drink differently (the UK counts "units" of 8 grams, for example), so a "drink" in one country's guidance isn't always the same as in another's.

## How to Estimate Your BAC: The Widmark Formula

The Widmark formula is the basis of most BAC calculators. A simple version looks like this:

**Estimated BAC (%) = [grams of alcohol ÷ (body weight in grams × r)] × 100 − (0.015 × hours since you started drinking)**

Here, **r** is a factor that represents how much of your body is water that alcohol can spread into. Commonly used values are about 0.68 for men and 0.55 for women. The 0.015 is an average rate at which BAC falls per hour.

### Example 1

A 180-pound man (about 81,600 grams) has four standard drinks (4 × 14 = 56 grams of alcohol) over two hours.

- 81,600 × 0.68 = about 55,500
- 56 ÷ 55,500 × 100 = about 0.10%
- 0.10% − (0.015 × 2) = about **0.07%**

### Example 2

A 140-pound woman (about 63,500 grams) has three standard drinks (42 grams) over two hours.

- 63,500 × 0.55 = about 34,900
- 42 ÷ 34,900 × 100 = about 0.12%
- 0.12% − (0.015 × 2) = about **0.09%**

Notice that she had one fewer drink but ended up higher. That's body size and body water at work.

### Why your real BAC may be different

The formula assumes all the alcohol is absorbed instantly and that your body clears it at an average rate. In real life:

- If you ate a big meal, your peak may be lower than the formula says.
- If you drank fast on an empty stomach, your BAC may still be climbing when the formula says it should be falling.
- Your own elimination rate might be faster or slower than 0.015% per hour.
- Drink sizes and strengths are almost always estimated, and usually underestimated.

Use the formula to understand the shape of what's happening, not to decide whether you're safe to drive.

## How Long Does It Take for BAC to Go Down?

Once alcohol is absorbed, your liver does almost all the work of removing it, mainly using an enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase. A small amount leaves through breath, sweat, and urine. The key point is that the liver works at a **roughly constant speed**. It doesn't go faster just because there's more alcohol to clear.

For most people, BAC falls by somewhere around 0.015% per hour on average, with a commonly cited range of about 0.010% to 0.020%. That gives a rough rule of thumb:

| Peak BAC | Approximate time to reach zero |
|---|---|
| 0.05% | About 3 to 4 hours |
| 0.08% | About 5 to 6 hours |
| 0.10% | About 6 to 7 hours |
| 0.15% | About 10 hours |
| 0.20% | About 13 hours |

This is why people who drink heavily until late at night can still be over the driving limit the next morning, even after sleeping. If you hit 0.15% at 1 a.m., you may not be fully clear until around 11 a.m. Feeling sober and being sober aren't the same thing.

### Things that don't lower your BAC

Because the liver sets the pace, none of the classic tricks work:

- **Coffee** can make you feel more alert, but it doesn't remove alcohol. You end up a wide-awake drunk person, which can be more dangerous because you feel more capable than you are.
- **Cold showers** wake you up but don't change your BAC.
- **Water** is good for you and can help with how you feel later, but it doesn't speed up alcohol removal from your blood.
- **Food after drinking** can't pull back alcohol that's already been absorbed, though it may slow absorption of anything still in your stomach.
- **Exercise or sweating** removes only a trivial amount.
- **Vomiting** only removes alcohol that hasn't been absorbed yet, and it's not something to do on purpose.

For a closer look at what does and doesn't affect alcohol clearance, see our guide on [how to speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism). The honest summary is that time is the only reliable fix.

## BAC and Hangovers: Why the Worst Part Comes Later

You might expect a hangover to be worst when your BAC is highest, but it works the other way around. Researchers generally describe a hangover as the set of symptoms that peaks around the time **BAC returns to roughly zero**. That's why you can go to bed feeling okay and wake up feeling awful.

A higher peak BAC tends to mean a worse hangover, though not for everyone. The causes are a mix of things that happen while alcohol is being processed: acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product of breaking down alcohol), dehydration from alcohol's effect on the hormone that helps you hold onto water, poor-quality sleep, irritation of the stomach lining, and an inflammatory response. Congeners, the extra compounds in darker drinks like whiskey and red wine, may add to it.

How long that lasts depends on how much you drank and how well you slept. Most hangovers fade within a day. Our guide to [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) goes into the timeline. And if you'd rather avoid the problem, the most effective strategies all come back to keeping your peak BAC lower: eating first, pacing yourself, alternating with water, and simply drinking less. We go through them in [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Alcohol Poisoning: When BAC Becomes an Emergency

Alcohol poisoning happens when BAC rises high enough to interfere with the parts of the brain that control breathing, heart rate, body temperature, and the gag reflex. It's most often the result of drinking a lot very quickly, like rapid shots or drinking games, because the BAC keeps climbing after the drinking stops.

The NIAAA lists these warning signs:

- Mental confusion or stupor
- Trouble staying conscious, or can't be woken
- Vomiting
- Seizures
- Slow breathing (fewer than 8 breaths a minute)
- Irregular breathing (10 seconds or more between breaths)
- Slow heart rate
- Clammy skin, pale or bluish skin
- Low body temperature

A person doesn't need to have all of these. If you see any of the serious ones, especially trouble breathing, unresponsiveness, or seizures, call 911.

### What to do while you wait for help

- **Stay with the person.** Don't leave them alone to sleep it off.
- **Keep them on their side** if they're lying down, so they won't choke if they vomit.
- **Don't give them coffee, food, or a cold shower.** None of these lower BAC, and some can make things worse.
- **Don't give them more alcohol** or any medication to "help them sleep."
- **Keep them warm**, since alcohol poisoning can lower body temperature.
- **Tell the responders what and how much they drank** if you know.

Many US states and colleges have "Good Samaritan" or medical amnesty policies meant to protect people who call for help in an alcohol emergency. Fear of getting in trouble should never stop you from calling.

## Common BAC Myths

**"I can tell when I'm at the limit."** Studies on self-assessment consistently find that people are poor judges of their own BAC, and that people who drink regularly can feel less drunk than they are. Alcohol impairs the very judgment you'd use to decide.

**"Beer won't get me as drunk as liquor."** A standard beer, a standard glass of wine, and a standard shot hold about the same alcohol. What matters is how much alcohol, not which kind.

**"Sleeping it off for a few hours makes me safe to drive."** Your liver clears alcohol at the same pace whether you're awake or asleep. A few hours of sleep after a heavy night may not be enough.

**"Breath mints or mouthwash can fool a breathalyzer."** Mints don't lower your BAC. Some mouthwashes contain alcohol and can briefly *raise* a breath reading.

**"Bigger people can drink as much as they want."** Body size changes how high your BAC goes per drink, but enough alcohol will impair anyone.

## Can Supplements Like DHM Lower Your BAC?

No product sold over the counter is a reliable way to lower your BAC, and nothing makes it safe to drive after drinking. That includes DHM (dihydromyricetin), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that is popular as a hangover supplement.

Some animal research has looked at whether DHM affects how alcohol acts on the brain and how quickly it is processed, and early studies in rodents were promising. Human evidence is still limited, and there is no good evidence that DHM meaningfully lowers BAC in people or reduces impairment at a given BAC. If you take DHM, think of it as something people use to feel better the next day, not as a way to sober up. You can read a balanced summary of the research in our [DHM science explainer](/never-hungover/dhm-science-explained).

If you do want to try it for the morning after, the two products we've looked at most closely are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which combines DHM with other ingredients like L-cysteine and electrolytes, and [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a lower-cost, DHM-only option. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how people typically take it. Either way, the things that actually keep your BAC down are the boring ones: eat first, pace your drinks, count standard drinks honestly, and give your liver time.

## The Bottom Line

BAC is the amount of alcohol in your blood, expressed as a percentage. It rises when you drink faster than your liver can clear alcohol, peaks 30 to 90 minutes after your last drink, and falls by roughly 0.015% per hour no matter what you do. Impairment starts well below the 0.08% driving limit, and around 0.30% and above, alcohol can become life-threatening. Your weight, sex, food, pace, and drink strength all shape how high your number climbs, which is why counting drinks is only a rough guide. If you're unsure, don't drive, and if someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, call for help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What does BAC mean?**

BAC stands for blood alcohol content, also called blood alcohol concentration. It's the amount of alcohol in your blood, shown as a percentage. A BAC of 0.08% means there are 0.08 grams of alcohol in every 100 milliliters of blood. It's the standard measure used for driving laws and medical care because it tracks closely with how impaired a person is.

**Is blood alcohol content the same as blood alcohol concentration?**

Yes. Blood alcohol content and blood alcohol concentration are two names for the same measurement, and both are shortened to BAC. You may also see it called blood alcohol level. Breath alcohol concentration (BrAC) is related but different: it's what a breathalyzer measures, which is then converted into an estimated BAC.

**What does a 0.08 BAC feel like?**

At 0.08%, most people feel noticeably buzzed or tipsy and may believe they're fine. In reality, coordination, balance, reaction time, reasoning, and the ability to judge speed and distance are all impaired. It's the legal driving limit for adults in most US states, but impairment begins well below it.

**How many drinks does it take to reach 0.08 BAC?**

It depends on your weight, sex, how fast you drink, and whether you've eaten. As a rough guide, many men around 180 pounds reach about 0.08% after four standard drinks in two hours, and many women around 140 pounds reach it after about three. Smaller people, people drinking on an empty stomach, and people drinking quickly can get there with fewer. Calculators and charts give estimates only.

**How long does it take for BAC to go down?**

On average, BAC falls by about 0.015% per hour, with a common range of roughly 0.010% to 0.020%. That means going from 0.08% to zero takes about five to six hours, and from 0.15% about ten hours. Sleep, coffee, water, and cold showers don't speed this up, because your liver clears alcohol at a roughly fixed pace.

**Can you lower your BAC quickly?**

No. Once alcohol is in your blood, your liver removes it at a fairly steady rate, and there's no food, drink, exercise, or supplement that meaningfully speeds that up. Coffee may make you feel more alert but leaves your BAC unchanged. Time is the only reliable way to bring BAC down.

**What BAC level is dangerous?**

Risk climbs steadily with BAC. Around 0.15% to 0.20%, vomiting and blackouts become likely. Around 0.30% and above, breathing and the gag reflex can be suppressed and a person may lose consciousness, which is a medical emergency. Levels of 0.40% and above can cause coma and death. Signs like slow or irregular breathing, seizures, or being unable to wake someone mean you should call 911.

**Does food lower your BAC?**

Eating before or while drinking lowers how high your BAC peaks, because food slows the rate at which alcohol moves from your stomach into your small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. Eating after you've already been drinking for a while can't remove alcohol that's already in your blood, though it can slow absorption of anything still in your stomach.

**Does DHM lower BAC?**

There is no good evidence that DHM meaningfully lowers blood alcohol content in people or makes you less impaired. Some animal studies looked at DHM's effects on alcohol, but human data is limited. DHM is used by some people for next-day hangover symptoms, not to sober up, and it never makes it safe to drive after drinking.
